title: Generalised anxiety disorder (adult)
subject: psychiatry
summary: Confirm GAD (excessive, hard-to-control worry for months with impairment), exclude medical and substance causes, and follow stepped care: education and monitoring, low-intensity CBT-based help, then CBT, applied relaxation or an SSRI (sertraline first); avoid long-term benzodiazepines and antipsychotics.

sections.title: Recognise and assess
items: Excessive, hard-to-control worry about several everyday matters on most days for at least 6 months, with restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension or poor sleep, causing distress or impairment.

Screen with the GAD-2 (feeling nervous, anxious or on edge; not being able to stop or control worrying); then use the GAD-7 to rate severity and track response (10 or more is a common threshold for probable GAD).
Consider GAD in frequent attenders who seek reassurance about physical symptoms or a chronic physical illness.
Assess comorbid depression, panic disorder, PTSD, OCD and alcohol or drug misuse. Treat the more severe or primary disorder first, and treat harmful alcohol or drug use first.
Exclude mimics: hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia, hypoglycaemia, excess caffeine, alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, stimulants, salbutamol and corticosteroids.
Ask about suicidal thoughts, especially with comorbid depression.

sections.title: Stepped care: steps 1 and 2 (NICE CG113)
items: Step 1 (everyone): explain the diagnosis, give information about GAD and treatment options, and actively monitor symptoms and function.
Step 2 (no improvement): low-intensity CBT-based help: non-facilitated self-help (at least 6 weeks), guided self-help (5 to 7 sessions) or psychoeducational groups (6 weekly sessions).
Discuss over-the-counter and herbal remedies: little evidence of benefit and a risk of interactions.

sections.title: Step 3: marked impairment or no response
items: Offer a choice of high-intensity psychological therapy (CBT or applied relaxation, usually 12 to 15 weekly 1-hour sessions) or drug treatment.

Drug treatment: offer an SSRI, with sertraline first (most cost-effective). If ineffective, offer another SSRI or an SNRI (for example escitalopram, duloxetine or venlafaxine), considering overdose toxicity (especially venlafaxine) and past response.
If SSRIs and SNRIs are not tolerated, consider pregabalin after checking for a history of drug misuse (dependence risk).
Do not offer a benzodiazepine except as a short-term measure during a crisis. Do not offer an antipsychotic for GAD in primary care.
No response to therapy: offer a drug; no response to a drug: offer therapy or another drug; partial response to a drug: consider adding therapy.

sections.title: Starting and monitoring drugs
items: Warn about early activation (more anxiety, agitation, poor sleep) and that the full effect develops over 1 week or more; starting at a low dose can help.
Under 30: warn about a possible increase in suicidal thinking with SSRIs and SNRIs; review within 1 week and monitor weekly for the first month.
Review effectiveness and side effects every 2 to 4 weeks for the first 3 months, then every 3 months. If effective, continue for at least 1 year because relapse is common.
SSRIs increase bleeding risk: consider gastroprotection in older people and those taking NSAIDs, aspirin or anticoagulants; check sodium in older adults.
Stop gradually to avoid withdrawal symptoms (see Depression in adults).

sections.title: Step 4: refer to specialist mental health services
items: Refer for severe anxiety with marked functional impairment plus risk of self-harm or suicide, significant comorbidity (substance misuse, personality disorder, complex physical illness), self-neglect, or inadequate response to step 3.
Specialist care offers a full review of past treatment adherence and fidelity, combined psychological and drug treatment, and other drug options.
Immediate risk: see Self-harm and suicide risk (adult).

sections.title: Special groups
items: Older adults: start low and go slow; watch for hyponatraemia, falls and interactions; avoid benzodiazepines (falls, confusion).
Pregnancy: prefer psychological therapy; if medication is needed, seek perinatal psychiatry advice and follow MHRA advice on pregabalin in pregnancy.

India: long-term benzodiazepine use (for example alprazolam or clonazepam) is common; plan a slow supervised taper rather than abrupt withdrawal. Tele-MANAS (14416) offers free tele-mental health support.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Long-term benzodiazepines: dependence, falls, cognitive impairment and road accidents; abrupt withdrawal can cause seizures.
Missing hyperthyroidism, alcohol withdrawal or stimulant use.
Stopping an SSRI after 1 to 2 weeks because of early worsening of anxiety.
Prescribing antipsychotics (such as low-dose quetiapine) for anxiety in primary care.
Missing comorbid depression and suicide risk.

drugs.name: Sertraline
drugs.dose: 25 to 50 mg orally once daily; increase in 50 mg steps at intervals of at least 1 week; max 200 mg daily
drugs.notes: NICE first choice (off-label for GAD in the UK). Start at 25 mg if very anxious.

drugs.name: Escitalopram
drugs.dose: 10 mg orally once daily; max 20 mg daily (65 or over: start 5 mg, max 10 mg)
drugs.notes: Licensed for GAD. QT prolongation at higher doses.

drugs.name: Duloxetine
drugs.dose: 30 to 60 mg orally once daily; max 120 mg daily
drugs.notes: Avoid in hepatic impairment and severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min); can raise blood pressure.

drugs.name: Venlafaxine (modified-release)
drugs.dose: 75 mg orally once daily; increase if needed; max 225 mg daily for GAD
drugs.notes: Monitor blood pressure; more toxic in overdose; withdrawal symptoms common.

drugs.name: Pregabalin
drugs.dose: 150 mg daily in 2 or 3 divided doses; increase by 150 mg daily at weekly intervals as needed; max 600 mg daily
drugs.notes: Reduce dose in renal impairment. Misuse and dependence; respiratory depression with opioids. Taper over at least 1 week.

drugs.name: Diazepam (crisis only)
drugs.dose: 2 mg orally up to three times daily for the shortest time, no more than 2 to 4 weeks; halve the dose in older adults
drugs.notes: Dependence, sedation, falls. Not for long-term treatment of GAD.

sources.title: Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113, updated 2020)
